request.system:
You revise one blog article for an online shop. You see the shop, the topic, the shop's products with the checked facts we hold about each (F1, F2…), the pages that may be linked, the current draft, and the problems found in it. Return the whole article again with every problem fixed. Where a sentence cannot be backed by a fact, remove it or say less; never add a citation the fact does not support. Keep what was good.

How to write it:
- In English, in the shop's tone, for the shop's audience. 700–2000 words. Open with a short paragraph that answers the search directly, then the sections as "##" headings ("###" below them if needed). No "#" heading: the title is set separately. Use a list or a table where it genuinely helps the reader. Write Markdown only, never HTML.
- You may speak as the shop ("in our range", "we stock"). Never claim experience: no testing, trying, favourites, "in our experience", what customers say, and no "I".
- Never mention a price, a discount, delivery, competitors or other shops. Respect the never-say list.

Every product claim cites its facts. After any sentence that says something about one of our products, put the facts it rests on in square brackets just before the full stop: "It is dishwasher safe [F5]." or "[F2, F7]". The sentence may say only what those facts say. Every sentence that names one of our products needs a citation.

Add nothing to a fact: no benefit, cause, consequence or comparison it does not state itself, however likely it seems. If a fact says the strainer has two ears, do not write that the ears rest on the mug's rim; if a fact says a tin holds 100 g of tea, do not write that a 60 g bag fits in it; if a fact says the grinder has 30 settings, do not write that this makes it easy to dial in. State the fact plainly, and put any general advice in its own sentence that does not name the product.

Numbers. A number about our products must appear in a fact the sentence cites. A number that is general knowledge, not about our products (a common ratio, temperature or time), is allowed only if it is well established and uncontroversial; mark its sentence with [G] before the full stop, and do not name any of our products in that sentence. Never invent statistics, studies or survey figures. Headings carry no brackets, so keep numbers out of headings unless they count the article's own items.

Links and products. Link only to the pages and products you were given, by their reference as the address: [our ceramic dripper](P1), [our brewing guide](L2). Never write a web address. To show a product card, put {{P1}} alone on its own line where the card should appear; show each card once.

Before you answer, read every sentence once more. A sentence with a digit in it carries [F…] for a fact that contains that number, or [G]. A sentence that names one of our products, even just to recommend it, carries [F…]. Fix any that do not.

Also give: meta_description, 70–170 characters, plain, no brackets; slug, lowercase words joined by hyphens.

Title: Long Leash for Recall: How to Use a Long Line to Train a Reliable Come
Meta description: Learn how to use a long leash for recall training: what to look for in a long line, harness tips, step-by-step drills and safe line handling.
Slug: long-leash-for-recall-training

The best way to use a long leash for recall is as a safety net, not a tow rope. Clip it to a well-fitted harness and let your dog explore at a distance. Call once in a happy voice, then reward generously every time they come back. With a long line attached, a missed recall never turns into a runaway, so your dog keeps practising getting it right. Below, we cover what to look for in a long line, how to attach it, a simple drill plan and how to handle the line safely.

## Why a long leash makes recall training safer

There's a big gap between a regular leash walk and true off-leash freedom. On a short leash, your dog never gets far enough away to really practise coming back. Off leash, one exciting squirrel can undo weeks of work, and every time your dog ignores a cue and gets away with it, that habit gets a little stronger.

A long line bridges that gap. Your dog gets room to sniff, wander and make choices at a distance, just like they would off leash. You can still step on or gather the line to stop a run-off, and you can gently guide them back if they don't respond. That way, the come cue keeps meaning one thing: coming back to you is always worth it.

That's the job our [Training Long Line](P1) is made for. It's a 30 ft leash made by Northpaw and intended for recall practice [F1, F2, F3, F5].

{{P1}}

## What to look for in a long line for recall

Not every long leash is a good recall tool. Here's what matters most:

- **Length:** You want enough room to practise real distance, but not so much line that it becomes a tangled mess you can't manage.
- **Weight:** A heavy line drags on your dog and tires your arms. Lighter is easier for both of you.
- **Material:** Long lines spend a lot of time on grass, mud and wet ground. A material that wipes clean and doesn't get waterlogged stays pleasant to handle.
- **Clip:** The clip is your connection to your dog, so it needs to be secure and sturdy. A swivel helps reduce twisting as your dog moves around.

Here's how our Training Long Line measures up on these points [F1, F4, F7, F8]:

| Feature | Training Long Line |
|---|---|
| Length | 30 ft [F1] |
| Material | Lightweight biothane [F4] |
| In water | Floats [F7] |
| Clip | Stainless steel swivel clip [F8] |
| Handle | No handle loop [F6] |

The missing handle loop is worth knowing about before you choose a line [F6]. Some owners like a loop to grip, while others prefer a plain line that has nothing to catch on roots or branches as it drags. Think about how you like to hold a line before you decide.

## Attach it to a harness, not a collar

If your dog bolts and hits the end of a long line at speed, a collar puts all of that force on the neck. A well-fitted harness spreads the load across the chest and shoulders, which makes it the safer attachment point for long-line work.

Fit is everything. A good harness shouldn't rub behind the front legs, shouldn't slide around when your dog moves, and should let you slip a couple of fingers under the straps without being loose. Measure your dog's chest girth rather than guessing, and recheck the fit as your dog grows or changes shape.

Our [Front-Clip No-Pull Harness](P2) comes in sizes XS, S, M, L and XL, fitting a chest girth of 13–42 in across the range [F11, F16]. It has four adjustment points and a padded neoprene chest plate [F13, F14]. For everyday walks, it also has a leash ring on the chest that turns the dog sideways when it pulls [F12].

Not sure which style suits your dog? Our guide on [how to choose a dog harness](L3) walks through the options, and the [harness size guide](L6) helps you measure and pick the right size.

{{P2}}

## Step-by-step recall drills on a long line

Recall is built in small, easy wins. Keep sessions short and fun, and move to the next step only when your dog is nailing the current one.

### Step one: start close in a quiet space

Pick a calm spot with few distractions, like your garden or an empty field. Keep most of the line gathered up so your dog is only a short distance away. Let them wander and sniff, then call your cue once in a bright, happy voice.

### Step two: reward like you mean it

When your dog reaches you, throw a party. Use their favourite treats, a game of tug or lots of praise. Gently take hold of the harness for a second before releasing them to go play again, so coming back doesn't always mean the fun is over.

### Step three: let out more line

Once your dog is coming back reliably at short range, gradually let out more line and call from further away. Over time, you can work up toward the full 30 ft of the Training Long Line [F1]. If your dog doesn't respond, avoid repeating the cue over and over. Instead, make an encouraging sound, move away from them, or gently guide them in with the line, then reward when they arrive.

### Step four: add mild distractions

When distance is going well, add small challenges: a toy lying on the grass, a person walking past at a distance, or a new location. Make each step only slightly harder than the last. If your dog struggles, go back a step and build up again.

### Tips that make recall stick

- **Never call your dog to something unpleasant.** If you need to clip on a leash to leave the park, give a bath or trim nails, go and get your dog instead of calling.
- **Call once.** Repeating the cue teaches your dog that the first call is optional.
- **End on a success.** Finish each session with an easy recall your dog gets right, so you both walk away feeling good.
- **Keep it varied.** Mix up rewards and locations so recall stays exciting.

## Handling the line safely

A long line is a great tool, but it needs a little care to use safely:

- **Keep slack off the ground near your feet.** Loops of line around your ankles are easy to trip over.
- **Never wrap the line around your hands or fingers.** If your dog takes off, a wrapped line can tighten fast and cause injury.
- **Consider gloves.** They protect your hands if the line slides through them.
- **Let the line drag only in open, safe areas.** A trailing line can snag, and it's harder to grab in long grass or brush.
- **Watch for tangles.** Keep an eye on the line around your dog's legs, trees, posts and other dogs, and stop to untangle before it tightens.

Our Training Long Line is made of lightweight biothane and floats in water [F4, F7]. If you train near ponds or streams, it's worth knowing how your line behaves in water before your dog decides to go for a swim. Also remember that the Training Long Line has no handle loop [F6]. Hold the line itself in a relaxed grip, with any extra length gathered loosely in your other hand.

## From long line back to everyday leash

So when can you start relying less on the long line? Look for consistency. Your dog should come back quickly the first time you call, at full line length, in different places and with real distractions around. When that's happening most of the time, you can try letting the line drag in a safe, open area so you can still grab it if needed. Stay patient, though. Reliable recall often takes many months of practice, and going back to the long line in new or exciting places is completely normal.

Even with a great recall, a standard leash still belongs in your walking kit. Streets, busy paths and places where dogs must be leashed call for something shorter and easier to manage up close.

Our [Biothane Leash](P3) is 6 ft long and made of coated webbing that does not absorb water or smell [F17, F18]. It can be wiped clean and has a breaking strength of 600 lb [F21, F22].

{{P3}}

Wondering which length suits which situation? Our [dog leash length guide](L4) compares shorter leashes with long lines. You can also browse all our [walking gear](L1) to put together a kit for both recall training and everyday walks.

With a long line, a comfy harness and plenty of happy practice, you're giving your dog the best chance at a recall you can truly count on. Happy training!
